Moving from NACHO 2

Source: vignettes/articles/moving-from-nacho-2.Rmd
moving-from-nacho-2.Rmd

NACHO 3 stores a study in one nacho object, where NACHO 2 used a list with a long $nacho table. This article is for you if you have NACHO 2 code, saved NACHO 2 objects, or a pipeline that calls NACHO 2. It shows how to convert your objects, which calls change, and which results change.

You do not have to move. NACHO 2.0.8 keeps working with the code you have. If you stay, pin the version, for example with renv::install("NACHO@2.0.8"). NACHO 3 needs R 4.3 or newer.

library(NACHO)

Saved objects

A NACHO 2 object saved with saveRDS() does not work as a NACHO 3 object. read_nacho() reads a saved file from any NACHO version, and converts NACHO 2 objects on the way. upgrade_nacho() converts an object that is already in your R session.

old <- readRDS("nacho-2-object.rds")
nacho <- upgrade_nacho(old)

nacho <- read_nacho("nacho-2-object.rds")

The conversion keeps the raw counts, the sample sheet, the settings and the thresholds. It computes the quality-control metrics, the normalised counts, the PCA and the outlier flags again, with the NACHO 3 definitions. It also moves the object to the legacy preset, with background = "geo", background_mode = "subtract" when the panel has negative probes, so the flags and the background correction stay close to what NACHO 2 gave you. Housekeeping genes that NACHO 2 predicted are kept as fixed genes and are not predicted again, so the geNorm change does not affect a converted object. The numbers can still differ slightly, because of the changes listed in the section on results. Only read files you trust, since readRDS() can run code stored in a file.

read_nacho() also reads NACHO 3 objects, and upgrade_nacho() returns a NACHO 3 object unchanged. GSE74821 is already a NACHO 3 object, so this call changes nothing.

identical(upgrade_nacho(GSE74821), GSE74821)
#> `x` is already a NACHO 3 object, so it is returned unchanged.
#> [1] TRUE

Function and object changes

The table gives the NACHO 3 call for each NACHO 2 call. Read x as a nacho object.

NACHO 2 NACHO 3
x$nacho, the long table as.data.frame(x, long = TRUE).
The Count column of x$nacho nacho_counts(x), a matrix with one row per probe and one column per sample.
The Count_Norm column of x$nacho nacho_counts(x, normalised = TRUE).
The sample columns of x$nacho nacho_samples(x), one row per sample.
The probe columns of x$nacho nacho_probes(x), one row per probe.
Other elements, such as x$housekeeping_genes and x$normalisation_method x@settings, for example x@settings[["housekeeping_genes"]]. print(x) gives a summary.
x$outliers_thresholds nacho_thresholds() builds a set of limits, and x@thresholds holds the ones in use.
The is_outlier column of x$nacho nacho_qc(x)[["status"]], with one status per metric, n_flags and reason beside it.
check_outliers() Removed, since the status always follows the thresholds of the object.
normalise(x, remove_outliers = TRUE) exclude_outliers(x).
autoplot(x, x = "BD") autoplot(x, type = "BD").
render(x, output_file = , show_outliers = , clean = ) render(x, format, output_dir, title, author, group).
visualise(x), which saved nacho_object.rds in tempdir() visualise(x) returns the tuned object, and writes no file.
deploy(), which defaulted to /srv/shiny-server deploy(directory = ), with no default.

NACHO 2 had no x$raw_counts and no x$normalised_counts, although some old documentation said so. The raw and normalised counts were the Count and Count_Norm columns of x$nacho.

Counts and tables

nacho_counts() returns a matrix, so the long table is no longer the way in. as.data.frame(x, long = TRUE) gives the long layout back when you need it for ggplot2 or dplyr.

dim(nacho_counts(GSE74821))
#> [1] 72 48
dim(nacho_counts(GSE74821, normalised = TRUE))
#> [1] 72 48
dim(as.data.frame(GSE74821, long = TRUE))
#> [1] 3456   87

In NACHO 2, x$nacho repeated the sample columns on every probe row. In NACHO 3, nacho_samples() and nacho_probes() keep them apart.

Outlier flags

nacho_qc() gives one row per sample. Each metric has its own status column, and status, n_flags and reason sum them up. The limits come from nacho_thresholds(), and x keeps them, so there is no check_outliers() to run.

head(nacho_qc(GSE74821)[, c("IDFILE", "status", "n_flags", "reason")], n = 3)
#>                                                               IDFILE status
#> 1 GSM1934697_20111102_20111102-9741-1_LGWU101986-1036378WU_02.RCC.gz   pass
#> 2 GSM1934698_20111102_20111102-9741-1_LGWU102547-1036381WU_05.RCC.gz   pass
#> 3 GSM1934699_20111102_20111102-9741-1_LGWU102569-1036382WU_06.RCC.gz   pass
#>   n_flags reason
#> 1       0   <NA>
#> 2       0   <NA>
#> 3       0   <NA>

exclude_outliers() drops the flagged samples and normalises the others again. normalise() has no remove_outliers argument any more. When no sample is flagged, exclude_outliers() says so and returns the object.

nacho <- exclude_outliers(GSE74821)
#> No sample is flagged, so nothing is removed.
dim(nacho_counts(nacho))
#> [1] 72 48

Plots

autoplot() takes the plot name in type. NACHO 3 stops when you pass x, and the error says that x was renamed type.

autoplot(GSE74821, type = "BD")

autoplot(GSE74821, x = "BD")

Reports

render() writes a Quarto report, and the old arguments are gone. output_file and clean have no replacement: the file is nacho-report.html or nacho-report.pdf in output_dir, and the working files live in a temporary folder. show_outliers has no replacement either. The report settings outliers_factor and outliers_labels still change how flagged samples look. The report needs the Quarto command-line interface 1.9.18 or newer. Use format = "typst" for a PDF, which needs no LaTeX. render() returns the path of the report.

path <- render(
  GSE74821,
  format = "html",
  output_dir = "reports",
  title = "Quality control of GSE74821",
  author = "Jane Doe, Genomics Core"
)

The first argument is now x, so change render(nacho_object = ...) to render(x = ...) or drop the name. title, author and group are new. With group, which names a column of nacho_samples(x), the report checks whether the batches and the biological groups are confounded.

The app

visualise() opens the app and returns the tuned object when you click Done. nacho_app() returns a Shiny app object, and deploy() copies an app.R that calls nacho_app() into directory/app_name. deploy() no longer defaults to /srv/shiny-server, so pass directory. Read Explore quality control in the app for a tour of the pages.

tuned <- visualise(GSE74821)
deploy(directory = "/srv/shiny-server")

Results that change

The same data can give different numbers in NACHO 3. These changes come from corrections of the methods, not from the new class.

  • The PCA is computed again with the NACHO 3 code, so the components can differ.
  • Normalised counts are no longer rounded, and no longer floored at 0.1.
  • There is no background correction by default, which is background = "none". Choose a statistic with background and whether to threshold or subtract with background_mode. Subtracting floors the counts at 0.
  • Samples are flagged against the nSolver thresholds by default, where NACHO 2 used its own limits.
  • Negative probes are excluded with Bruker’s rule, which drops at most two probes that are 3-fold above the others.
  • The positive control linearity leaves out POS_F and adds 1 to every count in the nSolver preset.
  • Negative_factor is always the geometric mean of the kept negative controls, also with normalisation_method = "GLM". NACHO 2 subtracted the model intercept, so GLM-normalised counts differ. The background applied sits in the new Background column.
  • housekeeping_predict = TRUE picks the five most stable genes by geNorm, among the genes above background in at least 90% of the samples. NACHO 2 picked the five genes with the smallest spread.
  • miRNA panels are no longer normalised with housekeeping genes by default. Give housekeeping_genes, or set housekeeping_norm = TRUE or housekeeping_predict = TRUE, to turn it back on.
  • Plots use the NACHO theme, and the shared labels use US spelling, such as “Normalized” and “Hemolysis”.

NACHO 2 outlier calls

The legacy preset keeps the NACHO 2 limits. With background = "geo", background_mode = "subtract", it gives back the NACHO 2 outlier calls. A converted object already has these settings. For a NACHO 3 object, pass them to normalise().

legacy <- normalise(
  GSE74821,
  outliers_thresholds = nacho_thresholds(preset = "legacy"),
  background = "geo",
  background_mode = "subtract"
)
#> Normalising again with new settings:
#> • background
#> • background_mode
#> • thresholds preset
table(nacho_qc(legacy)[["status"]])
#> 
#> pass 
#>   48

For new data, pass the preset and the background to load_rcc(), because its default is background = "none". The limits of the preset are the defaults NACHO 2 stored in x$outliers_thresholds.

load_rcc(data_directory, ssheet_csv, preset = "legacy", background = "geo", background_mode = "subtract")
str(nacho_thresholds(preset = "legacy"), max.level = 1)
#> List of 13
#>  $ preset               : chr "legacy"
#>  $ instrument           : chr "max"
#>  $ BD                   : num [1:2] 0.1 2.25
#>  $ FoV                  : num 75
#>  $ PCL                  : num 0.95
#>  $ LoD                  : num 2
#>  $ Positive_factor      : num [1:2] 0.25 4
#>  $ House_factor         : num [1:2] 0.0909 11
#>  $ Housekeeping_detected: num 0
#>  $ Ligation_order       : num 0
#>  $ Ligation_R2          : num 0
#>  $ Ligation_NEG         : num [1:2] -Inf Inf
#>  $ Haemolysis           : num [1:2] -Inf Inf

Pipelines

Two nf-core modules, nacho/qc and nacho/normalize, which the nf-core/nanostring pipeline uses, call NACHO 2 code. They read list elements such as [["nacho"]], [["outliers_thresholds"]] and [["housekeeping_genes"]], and call autoplot(x = ) and render(output_file = , show_outliers = ). In NACHO 3, x[["..."]] fails with the error S7 objects are not subsettable, and the two calls fail as described above. The modules pin NACHO 2.0.7, so they keep working until they update. This section was checked on 11 October 2026 against nf-core/modules, whose nacho modules pin NACHO 2.0.7.

Module call NACHO 3 replacement
[["nacho"]], with Count_Norm pivoted to a wide table nacho_counts(x, normalised = TRUE).
[["outliers_thresholds"]] and the PASS or FAIL table the module builds by hand x@thresholds and the *_status columns of nacho_qc(x).
[["housekeeping_genes"]] x@settings[["housekeeping_genes"]].
autoplot(x, x = "BD") autoplot(x, type = "BD").
render(x, output_file = "report.html", show_outliers = TRUE) render(x, output_dir = "reports"), which writes reports/nacho-report.html.

The call to load_rcc() in the modules uses no preset or background, so NACHO 3 gives it the nSolver preset with no background correction. The numbers change even where the calls still run. To keep the NACHO 2 results, pass preset = "legacy", background = "geo", background_mode = "subtract", as shown in the section on NACHO 2 outlier calls.

The nacho/qc module renders twice, to two file names. In NACHO 3 both reports are called nacho-report.html, so the second overwrites the first unless you give each call its own output_dir. Rename or move the report in the next step of the pipeline if it expects another file name.
